About
I study the economics of livestock production and marketing, with a focus on the Intermountain West. My extension program delivers practical economic analysis to producers and industry stakeholders across the region.
I attended BYU-Idaho, Purdue, and completed my Ph.D. at Kansas State University. I was raised in rural Idaho, surrounded by agriculture, and that practical background continues to inform my work.

title: The Economics of AI and Employment: Why Mass Unemployment is Unlikely
text: Public concern about artificial intelligence displacing workers follows a pattern from economic history. The power loom, the steam engine, the assembly line, and the personal computer each prompted similar predictions of widespread job loss. In each case, the technology did displace workers from specific tasks, but the aggregate employment consequences were typically positive because cost reductions also expanded output and generated demand for labor. Whether AI follows the same path remains an open question. However, there are reasons to be optimistic. This blog post walks through an economic framework to help clarify what happens when production technology changes.

title: The Economics of AI and Employment: Why Mass Unemployment is Unlikely
text:
A General Production Framework
Consider a representative economy producing output \(Y\) using capital (remember this is the stock of productive assets—not money) \(K\) and labor \(L\):
\[Y = F(K, L)\]
where \(F\) satisfies standard neoclassical properties: \(F_K, F_L > 0\) and \(F_{KK}, F_{LL} < 0\). In competitive input markets, factors are paid their marginal products (wages and rents in this case):
\[w = F_L(K, L) \qquad r = F_K(K, L)\]

title: The Economics of AI and Employment: Why Mass Unemployment is Unlikely
section: AI as a Shift in Relative Marginal Products
text:
AI as a Shift in Relative Marginal Products
AI can be modeled as a capital-augmenting technological shock that raises the effective productivity of capital relative to labor. Let \(\theta > 0\) represent this increase in effective productivity:
\[Y = F(\theta K, L)\]
As \(\theta\) increases, the marginal product of capital rises and the relative marginal product of labor falls:
\[MPK = \theta \cdot F_K(\theta K, L) \uparrow \qquad \frac{MPL}{MPK} \downarrow\]
This change has two simultaneous effects: it lowers the relative cost of using capital, and it lowers the marginal cost of producing output, as capital is substituted for labor. Each of these effects impact labor demand in opposite directions.

title: The Economics of AI and Employment: Why Mass Unemployment is Unlikely
text:
Decomposing the Labor Demand Response
The total effect on labor demand can be decomposed as:
\[\frac{dL}{d\theta} = \underbrace{\left.\frac{\partial L}{\partial \theta}\right|_{\bar{Y}}}_{\text{Substitution Effect } (-)} + \underbrace{\frac{\partial L}{\partial Y} \cdot \frac{dY}{d\theta}}_{\text{Output Effect } (+)}\]
The substitution effect on labor is negative: holding output constant, the relatively lower cost of capital induces firms to substitute toward \(K\) and away from \(L\). This substitution pushes labor demand downward.
The output effect is positive: AI-driven cost reductions expand equilibrium output \(Y^*\), and since \(\partial L / \partial Y > 0\), this scale expansion pulls labor demand upward.
The net effect on employment is theoretically indeterminate, with pressure in both directions.

title: The Economics of AI and Employment: Why Mass Unemployment is Unlikely
section: Substitution or Output: The Historical Record
text:
Substitution or Output: The Historical Record
Here are some historical examples of technilogical change where the output effect dominated:
Agricultural mechanization in the 19th and 20th centuries displaced the large majority of the agricultural workforce in developed economies. In 1900, roughly 41% of the American labor force worked in agriculture; today the figure is less than 2% (Dimitri, Effland, and Conklin, 2005). Total employment did not decline; labor reallocated into manufacturing and services, with real wages rising over the same period.
Electrification in the early 20th century is perhaps the closest historical analogue to AI: a general-purpose technology that augmented capital productivity across virtually every sector simultaneously. Factories reorganized around the new technology, displacing many workers, yet the decades following broad electrification saw robust wage growth in manufacturing, as productivity gains raised the marginal product of the remaining workers and created new consumer goods industries (David, 1990).
The computing and internet revolution produced similar concerns in the 1980s and 1990s. Spreadsheet software was widely expected to displace bookkeepers and accounting clerks by automating routine calculations. Instead, employment in accounting and financial analysis grew substantially in the decades following the spreadsheet’s adoption, because lower calculation costs increased the demand for financial analysis and expanded the range of decisions firms could address quantitatively — raising demand for workers who could interpret and act on that analysis (Bessen, 2015).
The pattern across these and other examples is amazingly consistent. Technological improvements have lowered production costs and almost always generated more aggregate labor demand, even as tasks are increasingly done by machines. And it didn’t matter if the tasks were physical or cognitive in nature — aggregate employment declines that were predicted did not materialize.

title: The Economics of AI and Employment: Why Mass Unemployment is Unlikely
text:
Conclusion
Discussions of the future of labor in the age of AI are often one sided, focusing on job losses. However, Economic theory is clear that there are positive and negative impacts of new technology. History suggests that the positive almost always outweighs the negative. Many argue that the AI revolution is “unprecedented”, but so too were each of the previously discussed technological revolutions. And the economic fundamentals are not so different as they might seem at first.
On balance, the economics and historical evidence suggests that mass unemployment from AI is unlikely.

title: When the River Runs Low: How Transportation Disruptions Affect Local Grain Basis
text:
My coauthors at the University of Arkansas and I recently published a paper in Agribusiness on how transportation cost shocks along the Mississippi River system affect corn and soybean basis (full article: https://doi.org/10.1002/agr.70108). Here is the abstract:

A substantial share of U.S. soybean and corn exports from the Midwest moves by barge along the Mississippi River system to export terminals in the Louisiana Gulf. Transportation costs between Midwestern grain elevators and export terminals create a wedge between prices at these locations, and shocks to these costs are partially passed on to farmers through lower cash bids and weaker basis. We estimate the pass-through rate of river transportation cost shocks to farmers using elevator-level cash bids and barge freight rates in a fixed-effects instrumental variables model, with river levels serving as an instrument. We also examine interaction effects for distance to a river port, distance to a processing plant, and the density of nearby elevators. Results indicate that higher river transportation costs weaken soybean and corn basis. The negative effect is smaller for elevators located farther from a river port or in areas with more nearby elevators, while distance to a processing plant plays a limited role in mitigating barge rates being passed through to basis. Pass-through for corn is more strongly moderated by local elevator density, whereas pass-through for soybeans is more sensitive to distance from a river port. These findings help farmers assess their exposure to basis risk from river transportation disruptions. Our results also provide policymakers with an empirical measure of the cost of such disruptions on farmers, informing the valuation of infrastructure investments that mitigate them.

The work was motivated by historically low river levels late in the year — close to harvest time — over the last several years, which drove historically high barge freight rates (Figure 1).

Figure 1. Barge freight rates measured in USD per bushel of soybeans from Memphis, Tennessee.
Because river levels affect barge rates and are plausibly exogenous, we used them as an instrument to identify the relationship between barge rates and corn and soybean basis. River transportation costs do not affect every location the same way, though. We thought of a few reasons that farmers selling to a given elevator might be more or less exposed: proximity to a river port, proximity to alternative marketing options (ethanol plants, soy crush facilities, feed mills, etc.), and the density of nearby grain buyers (more competition for grain limits how much of the cost can be passed on). Figure 2 from the paper maps these features for corn.

Figure 2. Geographic distribution of corn elevators, river ports, gage sites, and processing plants within the Mississippi River Basin.
We found that pass-through of barge rates does indeed vary across these dimensions. The most intuitive result is that proximity to a river port increases the share of the cost passed on to farmers. Elevators located near processing plants that absorb local grain supply are more insulated from barge rate shocks. And greater spatial competition among grain buyers also limits pass-through. Figure 4 from the paper shows where the strongest (most negative) and weakest (least negative) impacts fall across the Mississippi River Basin.

Figure 4. Spatial distribution of marginal effects of barge freight rates on grain basis for corn. More negative values indicate stronger pass-through (e.g., a marginal pass-through of −0.35 means a $1 barge rate increase weakens basis by 35 cents). For corn, Iowa and southern Minnesota show weak pass-through due to competitive grain buying and abundant processing capacity, while the lower Mississippi shows strong pass-through due to limited competition and proximity to river ports.
What does this mean for real-life decision making? The most important implication is that river disruptions don’t just move the overall price level for commodities — reflected in the futures market — they also change basis. That distinction matters because basis risk is not easily hedged like general price risk. So determining your level of exposure to this risk is the first step in managing it.
The conclusion of the paper summarizes the implications this way:

Our findings highlight several implications. For producers, the results map shows where exposure to transportation disruptions is greatest. Strategies such as diversifying marketing and investment in storage capacity can help manage this source of basis risk. For policymakers, these results show the value to farmers of reliable river navigation. This value should be considered in the benefits of infrastructure investments to reduce navigation disruptions. Moreover, the role of competitive local grain buying markets in moderating cost transmission should be considered in merger review and rural development policy.

Check out the full article if you want more details on the background, methods, results, or implications!

title: The Economics of Herd Size During Drought
text:
Drought is an issue that Western ranchers are familiar with. While it is difficult to predict when drought will occur, it is certain that it will happen if you are in business for any significant amount of time. This year, 2026, happens to be one of those years in Utah. And for that matter, much of the rest of the country as shown in the US Drought Monitor map.
Managing during a drought means making important decisions about stocking rates, culling, feeding, and/or renting pasture. The first and most impactful decision is determining the drought-reduced carrying capacity of your existing forage base. This should be done with the goal to do no permanent damage to the ranch resources. When this determination is made, the next step is to determine the lowest cost (but still nutritionally acceptable) way to maintain the current herd size of the ranch. At this point you are now ready to answer the main question: should I reduce my herd?. There’s no universal right answer—it depends on your specific costs (especially hay/pasture rental), the cattle market, and the age demographics of your herd.
In this post, I am sharing a decision framework based on economic principles that I have developed along with my USU colleagues Ryan Larsen and David Secrist. We have also developed a decision tool that follows this framework, available at: farmanalysis.usu.edu.

title: When to Buy Feed, Lease Grass, or Sell the Cows
section: Start Here: A Cow Is a Capital Asset
text:
Start Here: A Cow Is a Capital Asset
This might sound like economist-speak, but it’s actually a useful way to think. A cow isn’t just an animal—she’s a machine that converts inputs (feed, water, health care, your time) into calves. And like any machine, she has a value based on what she’s expected to produce.
Economists call this net present value, or NPV. The NPV of a cow is the total expected profit from her future calves—discounted back to today’s dollars—plus whatever she’ll be worth when you eventually sell her as a cull. It depends on:

Expected calf prices
How much her calves weigh at weaning
The probability she actually weans a calf (pregnancy rate × calving rate × survival)
The annual cost of keeping her (feed, vet, labor, breeding)
What she’ll bring at the salebarn at the end of her productive life

The key insight is that every cow’s NPV is different. A healthy, proven 5-year-old has a higher NPV than a 12-year-old with declining weaning rates. Age isn’t a perfect predictor, but it’s a very good one.

title: When to Buy Feed, Lease Grass, or Sell the Cows
text:
The Basic Decision Rule (Normal Year)
In a normal year, the culling decision comes down to a comparison:

Retain if: the cow’s NPV > her current market value, minus the cost of eventually replacing her.

Why does replacement cost matter? Because if you sell a cow today and need to rebuild the herd later—especially when cattle prices are high—that replacement will cost you. That expected future cost chips away at the benefit of selling now. If it’s expensive to rebuild later, you need a pretty good reason to sell today.
Flip it around and you get the sell signal: if a cow’s NPV is low enough that her current market value (net of that replacement penalty) exceeds what she’d produce for you, she should go.
In practice, you can rank cows by expected NPV (again, age is a useful proxy) and work from the bottom up: oldest and least productive go first.

title: When to Buy Feed, Lease Grass, or Sell the Cows
text:
What Drought Changes
Drought doesn’t change the basic logic—it just adds costs.
Those costs come in two layers. First, herd-wide drought costs: higher hay prices, hauled water, extra labor. These hit every cow in the herd whether the ranch is overstocked or not. Second, over-capacity costs: once you’re running more cows than the drought-reduced range can support, you’re buying supplemental feed for every head above that reduced carrying capacity.
The decision equation in a drought year becomes:

Retain if: the cow’s NPV minus drought costs > her current market value, minus the replacement penalty.

This is the same comparison as before—it’s just that drought costs are now eating into the NPV side of the equation. A cow who was worth keeping in a normal year may not be worth keeping once you account for what the drought is costing you to keep her around.
You can also solve this equation for what we call D*: the breakeven drought cost, or the maximum drought cost a given cow can absorb before the sell decision becomes rational. Cows with higher NPV have more buffer—they can absorb more drought cost before it makes sense to sell. Cows with lower NPV (older animals, poorer producers) hit that breakeven faster.

title: When to Buy Feed, Lease Grass, or Sell the Cows
text:
The Carrying Capacity Problem
Drought also shrinks the land’s carrying capacity. If you normally run 400 cows across a mix of spring permits, summer range, and fall aftermath, a severe drought might cut your summer and fall capacity by half. That’s roughly 36,000 fewer animal-unit-days of grazing—meaning you’d need to cover that gap with purchased feed, leased pasture, or fewer cows.
This is where the three options come back in:
Buy feed. Purchase hay or supplement to bridge the gap. This makes sense when feed prices are manageable and your cows’ NPV is high enough to cover the cost. It starts to fail when drought is widespread (so hay prices spike) or when you’re so far over capacity that the feed bill overwhelms any retention benefit.
Lease grass. Move cattle to leased pasture elsewhere. This preserves the herd but adds transportation, labor, and lease costs on top of everything else. It can be a good option if you can find grass at a reasonable price—but “finding reasonable grass during a drought” is its own challenge.
Sell cows. Cull down to drought carrying capacity. This locks in market value today but means rebuilding later, potentially at higher prices. For older cows with lower NPV, this is often the right call. For young, productive cows, it may not be—especially if replacement cost is going to be steep.

title: When to Buy Feed, Lease Grass, or Sell the Cows
section: The Graph: Where This All Comes Together
text:
The Graph: Where This All Comes Together
The figure below puts all of this in one place.



A stylized diagram showing the optimal cow herd size during drought. The downward-sloping curve is the Marginal NPV of cows in the herd. The two horizontal lines represent the cost thresholds that determine when to sell.


Here’s how to read it:
The Marginal NPV curve (the downward-sloping line) represents the value of adding one more cow to the herd. It slopes downward because of diminishing returns—the most productive cows are already in the herd, and each additional cow you retain is a bit less valuable than the last. This is also why you cull the least productive animals first: they’re at the bottom of this curve.
The Marginal Opportunity Cost (the lower flat line) is the hurdle you have to clear in a normal year. It represents the market value of a cow net of the replacement penalty—the opportunity cost of keeping her rather than selling her. In a normal year, you retain cows until the NPV curve crosses this line, which gives you the Normal Herd Size on the right side of the x-axis.
The Marginal Drought Cost + Opportunity Cost (the upper flat line) is the drought-adjusted hurdle. Once the herd exceeds the Carrying Capacity with Drought (the first vertical line), you’re buying supplemental feed for every additional cow—so the effective cost of retaining each additional animal jumps. The curve stays at the higher level until it hits the normal carrying capacity.
The Optimal Herd Size with Drought is where the NPV curve crosses the higher cost line. It sits between the drought carrying capacity and the normal herd size. This is the key result: during drought, you should run fewer cows than normal, but not necessarily as few as the drought range can support on its own. The optimal point is somewhere in between—and it depends on what your cows are worth versus what it costs to feed them through the drought.
The practical implication: if you’re sitting to the right of the optimal drought herd size, you have too many cows for current conditions. Every animal between the optimal and normal herd sizes is one where drought costs are exceeding the marginal NPV. Those animals should be sold—or their costs covered through feed or leased grass, if that pencils out.

title: When to Buy Feed, Lease Grass, or Sell the Cows
text:
Putting It Into Practice
You probably don’t have NPV estimates for each cow handy. Here’s the practical version:

Estimate your drought carrying capacity by season. Spring, summer, and fall may be affected differently. A 50% cut on your summer permit matters a lot more than a small reduction in spring pasture.
Calculate the deficit. The gap between your normal capacity and drought capacity tells you how many animal-unit-days you need to cover—whether through purchased feed, leased grass, or a smaller herd.
Price out all three options before committing to any one of them. Buy feed, lease grass, sell cows. Don’t assume one is always cheaper.
Work by age cohort. Rather than trying to estimate individual NPVs, group cows by age. Cull the oldest and least productive first. Three-year-olds and five-year-olds have a lot of productive life ahead—they can absorb more drought cost. Twelve-year-olds are much closer to their breakeven D*.
Run three price scenarios. Calf prices in a drought year can swing dramatically. Low, medium, and high forecast scenarios help you understand the range of outcomes and apply your own risk tolerance to the decision.
Monitor D* as drought costs accumulate. If supplemental feed prices spike mid-drought, recalculate whether the math still holds. The framework isn’t a one-time decision—it’s a running comparison.

title: When to Buy Feed, Lease Grass, or Sell the Cows
text:
The Bottom Line
Drought forces a decision that feels emotional but is fundamentally economic. The cows you keep need to be worth keeping—their expected future production needs to exceed what you’re spending to carry them through the drought, plus what you’d get by selling them today.
The framework here won’t make the decision for you. It won’t tell you what hay prices will do, or what calves will sell for next fall, or whether the drought will break in July. But it gives you a structure: compare NPV to effective market value, account for drought costs, find your breakeven, and cull from the bottom of the productivity ranking up.
A well-timed decision made from a framework beats a forced sale made from a crisis.

This post is based on ongoing research at Utah State University. Questions and feedback welcome at a.anderson@usu.edu. For more tools and resources, visit farmanalysis.usu.edu.

title: The Economics of Herd Size During Drought
section: A Cow Is a Capital Asset
text:
A Cow Is a Capital Asset
It is useful to think of your ranch as a factory and your cows as calf-producing machines within the factory. Using this analogy, both the ranch and the breeding stock are capital assets, something that you invest in for the promise of value creation for years to come. In this way of thinking, a cow has value based on what she’s expected to produce over her remaining lifespan.
Economists call this net present value, or NPV. The NPV of a cow is the total expected profit from her future calves—discounted back to today’s dollars—plus whatever she’ll be worth when you eventually sell her as a cull. It depends on:

Expected calf prices
How much her calves weigh at weaning
The probability she actually weans a calf (pregnancy rate × calving rate × survival)
The annual cost of keeping her (feed, vet, labor, breeding)
Cull value at the end of her productive life (adjusted for the possibility of premature death)

It is important to note that every cow’s NPV is different. A 5-year-old has a higher NPV than a 12-year-old because of (1) more expected calves, and (2) higher reproductive efficiency. However, we typically don’t have enough data to calculate individual animal NPVs, but a reasonable alternative is calculating NPV by age to help with our decision.

title: The Economics of Herd Size During Drought
text:
A Decision Rule (Normal Year)
In a normal year, the culling decision comes down to a comparison:

Retain if: the cow’s NPV > her current market cull value - excess replacement cost.

The left-hand side of the decision equation is the benefit of keeping the cow, while the right-hand side is the opportunity cost of that action. Economics always asks us to compare the benefits with the costs.
An opportunity cost is the value of the alternative we give up when making a choice. In this case, when we retain a cow, we cannot sell her in the cull market, so we forgo that potential revenue. There is also an adjustment for “excess replacement cost” because we will need to replace a cull to remain at a steady-state in terms of herd size. If we can purchase (or raise) a replacement at a price equal to their NPV, then this is not an issue. But if we have to pay a replacement cost above that animals expected NPV, then we need to factor this into the culling decision.

title: The Economics of Herd Size During Drought
text:
Decision Rule Under Drought Conditions
Drought doesn’t change the economic logic, it just adds costs.
There are two types of costs that are worth thinking about separately. First, herd-wide drought costs: higher hay prices, hauled water, extra labor. These apply to every cow in the herd whether the ranch is overstocked or not. Second, over-capacity costs: once you’re running more cows than the drought-reduced carrying capacity then you are buying supplemental feed for every animal above that reduced carrying capacity.
The decision equation in a drought year becomes:

Retain if: the cow’s NPV - drought costs > her current market cull value - excess replacement cost.

This is the same comparison as before, except drought costs are now reducing the benefit side of the equation (you could also add the costs to the cost side). A cow who was worth keeping in a normal year may not be worth keeping with the additional drought costs.

title: The Economics of Herd Size During Drought
text:
Thinking on the Margin
In addition to comparing costs and benefits, economics encourages us to “think on the margin”. The reason is that (under certain assumptions) evaluating the marginal cost and marginal benefit leads to profit maximizing decisions. But what does it mean to think on the margin? Well, “the margin” literally means the edge or border of something. In this case the margins of our herd.
To do this, we need to define the margin of the herd by ordering the cattle from the most to least valuable. The most valuable cattle come first, because they are the least likely to be culled. The ordering is important because it also allows us to apply costs to the correct cattle as well. For example, when the drought-reduced carrying capacity of the ranch is reached, the additional cost is applied to cattle over the threshold. And the cattle over the threshold are the least valuable cattle because of our ordering.

title: The Economics of Herd Size During Drought
text:
Bringing it Together Visually
There are few things economists love more than graphs because they can be effective in communicating abstract ideas. The concepts previously discussed are all brought together in the following graph.



The downward-sloping curve is the Marginal NPV (benefits) of cows in the herd. The horizontal curves are marginal costs. The intersection points are the optimal herd sizes with/without drought


Here’s how to read it:
The Marginal NPV curve this curve is downward sloping because we determined to order our herd by value, so that we cull the least valuable animals first.
The Marginal Opportunity Cost (the lower flat line) is the value of the animal in the cull market, or the revenue you give up by retaining her. It also includes the adjustment for excess replacement costs. In a normal year, you retain cows with NPVs that exceed this threshold, which gives you the Normal Herd Size on the right side of the x-axis.
The Marginal Drought Cost + Opportunity Cost (the upper flat line) is the drought-adjusted opportunity cost. Once the herd exceeds the Carrying Capacity with Drought (the first vertical line), you must purchase feed/pasture for every additional cow. We apply the per head costs only to the cows over the carrying capacity because they are causing the costs. This is what it means to “think on the margin”. In a drought year, the intersection of this line with the marginal NPV curve gives The Optimal Herd Size with Drought.
Depending where the lines fall, the best decision could be to sell cows, feed cows (or rent pasture), or a combination of these options. It depends on your operational specifics and the current and future cattle market.

title: The Economics of Herd Size During Drought
text:
Conclusion
If your drought situation is forcing you into the decision whether to sell cows or purchase hay, consider the economic principles in this post. We have also created a decision tool based on this framework to help you with the math for your operation. You can access it at: farmanalysis.usu.edu.
One thing to consider is that at current (and likely future) market prices, cattle NPVs are currently relatively high. This may make purchasing hay surprisingly worthwhile. It is certainly worth considering the options before reducing your herd.

Questions and feedback welcome at a.anderson@usu.edu. For more tools and resources, visit farmanalysis.usu.edu.
